title: Canvas Replication Instructions
section: How to (attempt to) replicate the Quarto demo in Canvas
text:
How to (attempt to) replicate the Quarto demo in Canvas
Follow these steps in your Canvas sandbox, then compare the result to the live course website. The gaps you encounter are the argument.


Before you start
Run demo-canvas-comparison.R in RStudio. It will produce two files in your working directory:

county_figure.png — the scatterplot
county_table.html — the formatted summary table




Step 1 — Create a Canvas Page

In your Canvas sandbox course, go to Pages → + Page
Title it: Descriptive Statistics: NC County Data
You now have the Rich Content Editor (RCE)




Step 2 — Try to add the R code
What you want: Show students the cleaning code with line-by-line annotations.
What Canvas gives you: - Paste the code into the RCE — it renders as plain paragraph text with no syntax highlighting - Switch to HTML view and wrap it in <pre><code> tags — you get monospaced text, still no highlighting, no hover annotations - There is no way to link a specific line of code to an explanatory tooltip
The gap: Students see raw text. They cannot tell which tokens are functions, which are arguments, and which are strings. There is no mechanism to annotate individual lines.



Step 3 — Try to add the summary table
What you want: A formatted table with a spanning header, currency-formatted numbers, and a footnote linked to a specific column.
Option A — Use the Canvas table tool: 1. In the RCE, click Insert → Table 2. Build the table manually, cell by cell 3. Notice: no column spanner rows, no footnote linking, no number formatting (you type “$56,300” by hand for every cell), no alternating row shading
Option B — Embed county_table.html: 1. Canvas does not allow embedding arbitrary HTML files in Pages 2. You can upload county_table.html to Files, but students download it as a file — it does not render inline on the page 3. You can take a screenshot of the table and upload it as an image — but screenshots have no semantic structure, fail screen readers, and cannot be resized without blurring
The gap: The Canvas table is a manual data-entry grid. It requires retyping every value, cannot format numbers programmatically, and has no support for grouped headers or linked footnotes. If the data change, every cell must be updated by hand.



Step 4 — Try to add the figure
What you want: An embedded, captioned, accessible figure with alt text.
What Canvas gives you: 1. In the RCE, click Insert → Images → Upload Image 2. Select county_figure.png and upload it 3. Canvas will prompt for alt text — type a description (most instructors skip this step, leaving the image inaccessible) 4. The figure appears on the page
What is missing: - The figure is a static image. If the data change, you must re-run the script, re-export, and re-upload manually - The caption is plain text typed below the image — it has no semantic connection to the figure (no <figcaption> element) - The alt text field is optional and unvalidated — there is no enforcement or reminder to complete it - There is no OLS trend line annotation or interactive tooltip
The gap: The figure works visually but is a dead end for pedagogy. Students cannot see the code that produced it, cannot reproduce it, and the page does not update if anything changes.



Step 5 — Compare
Open both side by side:



Feature
Canvas Page
Quarto Site




Syntax-highlighted code
✗
✓


Code + output on same page
✗
✓


Line-level code annotations
✗
✓


Formatted table (currency, %)
Manual entry
Automatic


Spanning column headers
✗
✓


Footnote linked to column
✗
✓


Semantic figure caption
✗
✓


Enforced alt text
✗
✓ (chunk option)


Updates when data change
Manual re-upload
Re-render once


Students can copy the code
✗
✓






The core argument
Canvas is a learning management system — it is designed for assignment submission, gradebooks, and announcements. It is not designed to serve as a pedagogical document for a methods course.
A Quarto site treats the course page itself as a reproducible document. The code, the output, and the explanation are co-located, version-controlled, and accessible by default. For a quantitative methods course where students are learning to read and write code, that difference is not cosmetic — it is the entire point.

title: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output
text:
The Scenario
You have received a dataset of county-level characteristics for 15 North Carolina counties. The data are messy: one value is missing and you need to derive a new categorical variable before producing summary statistics. Your task is to:

Inspect and clean the data
Produce a formatted descriptive statistics table broken down by region
Visualize the relationship between median household income and per capita public expenditure
crumbs: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output

title: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output
text:
Step 1 — Load and Inspect

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(scales)

# Simulated NC county data (representative values, not official statistics)
counties_raw <- tibble(
  county     = c("Wake", "Mecklenburg", "Guilford", "Forsyth", "Durham",
                 "Buncombe", "New Hanover", "Cumberland", "Gaston", "Onslow",
                 "Cabarrus", "Union", "Catawba", "Pitt", "Alamance"),
  region     = c("Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Piedmont",
                 "Mountains", "Coastal", "Coastal", "Piedmont", "Coastal",
                 "Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Coastal", "Piedmont"),
  population = c(1129410, 1115482, 541299, 382295, 330506,
                 275203, 234473, 335509, 228928, 207647,
                 218000, 245318, 159551, 177372, 169509),
  med_income = c(78500, 72100, 56300, 54200, 65800,
                 NA, 61400, 49300, 55200, 52100,
                 67300, 79200, 55600, 48700, 54100),
  unemp_rate = c(3.1, 3.4, 4.2, 4.5, 3.8,
                 3.9, 4.1, 5.2, 4.8, 6.1,
                 3.7, 3.2, 4.4, 5.0, 4.6),
  expend_pc  = c(3842, 4120, 3256, 3189, 4567,
                 2987, 3421, 2876, 2654, 2543,
                 3102, 3456, 2876, 2987, 2765)
)

glimpse(counties_raw)

Rows: 15
Columns: 6
$ county     <chr> "Wake", "Mecklenburg", "Guilford", "Forsyth", "Durham", "Bu…
$ region     <chr> "Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Piedmont", "Piedmont",…
$ population <dbl> 1129410, 1115482, 541299, 382295, 330506, 275203, 234473, 3…
$ med_income <dbl> 78500, 72100, 56300, 54200, 65800, NA, 61400, 49300, 55200,…
$ unemp_rate <dbl> 3.1, 3.4, 4.2, 4.5, 3.8, 3.9, 4.1, 5.2, 4.8, 6.1, 3.7, 3.2,…
$ expend_pc  <dbl> 3842, 4120, 3256, 3189, 4567, 2987, 3421, 2876, 2654, 2543,…


Notice that med_income for Buncombe County is NA. We handle this in the next step.
crumbs: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output

title: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output
text:
Step 2 — Clean the Data
The code below performs three operations. Hover over the numbered annotations to see what each does.

counties <- counties_raw |>
  mutate(
1    med_income = if_else(
      is.na(med_income),
      median(med_income, na.rm = TRUE),
      med_income
    ),
2    income_group = case_when(
      med_income >= 70000 ~ "High",
      med_income >= 55000 ~ "Middle",
      .default            = "Lower-Middle"
    ),
3    income_group = factor(
      income_group,
      levels = c("Lower-Middle", "Middle", "High")
    )
  )


1

Impute the missing value. Replaces the single NA in med_income with the column median. In a real analysis, document and justify this decision — median imputation is appropriate when missingness is isolated and the distribution is skewed.

2

Derive a categorical variable. case_when() is cleaner than nested if_else() calls when you have more than two conditions. The .default argument handles any cases not matched above.

3

Set factor level order. Without this step, R sorts categories alphabetically — putting “High” before “Lower-Middle” in tables and figures. Explicit level ordering ensures a logical sequence.
crumbs: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output

title: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output
text:
Step 3 — Descriptive Statistics Table






TipWhere a standard LMS may fall short



The table below has currency-formatted numbers, a spanning column header, a footnote linked to a specific column, and alternating row shading — all generated in a few lines of code. Producing a comparable table in Canvas typically requires manually entering every value into a basic HTML table editor, with limited support for number formatting, column groups, or linked footnotes.



counties |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    pop_avg    = mean(population),
    income_avg = mean(med_income),
    unemp_avg  = mean(unemp_rate),
    expend_avg = mean(expend_pc),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(region) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**County Characteristics by Region**"),
    subtitle = "Selected North Carolina Counties (Simulated Data)"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(
    label   = "Economic Characteristics",
    columns = c(income_avg, unemp_avg, expend_avg)
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    region     = "Region",
    n          = "N",
    pop_avg    = "Avg. Population",
    income_avg = "Median HH Income",
    unemp_avg  = "Unemployment (%)",
    expend_avg = "Expenditure per Capita"
  ) |>
  fmt_integer(columns = pop_avg) |>
  fmt_currency(columns = c(income_avg, expend_avg), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = unemp_avg, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_footnote(
    footnote  = "Income imputed for one county with missing data (median substitution).",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = income_avg)
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_fill(color = "#f8fafc"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = c(1, 3))
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style     = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_spanners()
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.width               = pct(100),
    heading.align             = "left",
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  )

title: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output
text:
Step 4 — Visualization

ggplot(
  counties,
  aes(x = med_income, y = expend_pc, color = region, size = population)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = 1),
    method   = "lm",
    se       = TRUE,
    color    = "#475569",
    linewidth = 0.6,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "K")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma_format(), range = c(3, 10)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Coastal"   = "#0ea5e9",
      "Mountains" = "#10b981",
      "Piedmont"  = "#6366f1"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Household Income and Per Capita Expenditure",
    subtitle = "15 Selected North Carolina Counties",
    x        = "Median Household Income",
    y        = "Per Capita Expenditure",
    color    = "Region",
    size     = "Population",
    caption  = "Source: Simulated data for instructional purposes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position  = "right",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )







Figure 1: A modest positive relationship exists between median household income and per capita expenditure. Piedmont counties span the widest income range; Coastal counties cluster at lower expenditure levels.
crumbs: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output

title: Descriptive Statistics: From Raw Data to Publication-Ready Output
text:
What This Demonstrates






ImportantFive areas where a dedicated course site has an advantage




Rendered code alongside its output. In a standard LMS, instructors typically paste screenshots of code and output as separate images. Students cannot easily copy, adapt, or verify the code from a screenshot.
Formatted statistical tables. The gt table above has currency formatting, a spanning column header, a footnote linked to a specific column, and conditional row shading — generated programmatically. Replicating this level of formatting in a basic HTML table editor is time-consuming and fragile.
Code annotations. The hover annotations in Step 2 link explanatory text directly to specific lines of code — a feature well-suited to methods instruction that is difficult to achieve in a page-based editor.
Accessible figure captions and alt text. The fig-cap and fig-alt chunk options produce a proper HTML <figcaption> and alt attribute as part of the authoring workflow, supporting WCAG compliance by default rather than as an afterthought.
Reproducibility. If the underlying data change, every table and figure on this page updates automatically on the next render. In a static page, each output would need to be manually regenerated and re-uploaded.
